name: Okayama & Kurashiki
tagline: Sunny-day gardens, a white-walled canal town and Seto Inland Sea fruit
intro: Built around Korakuen, one of Japan's three great gardens, and the Kurashiki Bikan Historical Quarter with its rows of white-walled storehouses, this destination also takes in Kibitsu Shrine (linked to the Momotaro legend) and views of the Seto Inland Sea, all within a day's reach. Known as the "Land of Sunshine" for its few rainy days, it is great for walking, and from summer to autumn fruit desserts made with white peaches and Muscat grapes are the highlight. It suits women travelers who enjoy a relaxed pace with cafes and sweets, and families with children.
season_notes: Spring: cherry blossoms along the Asahi River embankment and in Korakuen in early April, and fresh willow greenery along the Kurashiki canal. Summer: white peaches, Kyoho grapes and Muscat grapes are in season from July to September, with fruit parfaits and fruit picking (be sure to prepare for the heat). Autumn: the Seto Inland Sea fruit season winds down in October, and in late November there are autumn leaves at Korakuen and the autumn lanterns of the Kurashiki Bikan Quarter. Winter: clear, dry weather is good for walking, and Hinase oyster okonomiyaki (kakioko) is in season (November to March).
airport_access/0/note: Runs to match arriving flights, no reservation needed. Fares and times may have changed since 2025 (to be confirmed)
airport_access/1/note: Few runs per day, so checking the timetable is essential (to be confirmed)
airport_access/2/note: Convenient for groups of 3 to 4 with no waiting for the bus. Approximate
getting_around: In Okayama city, the streetcar from Okayama Station (¥120 per ride; get off at Joshita for Okayama Castle and Korakuen) and walking are enough. Kurashiki is 17 minutes (¥330) away on the JR Sanyo Main Line. Kibitsu Shrine is on the JR Kibi Line, Kojima and Washuzan are on the JR Seto-Ohashi Line, and Ushimado and Bizen are reached by the JR Ako Line plus a bus. Local lines run only once or twice an hour, so check the return timetable first. For the outskirts (Ushimado, Bitchu Matsuyama Castle and Hinase), a rental car is much easier.
transport_pass: Okaden streetcar 1-day pass ¥400 (to be confirmed). It pays off if you stay within the city, but on days you go out to Kurashiki or Kojima, buying regular JR tickets as you go is cheaper. There is no special pass for the Okayama Airport.
spots/0/desc: A small airport with direct flights from Incheon and Busan, about 18 km north of the city center. Limousine buses to Okayama Station leave from the stop right in front of the arrivals lobby.
spots/0/access: 30 minutes by limousine bus from the west exit of Okayama Station
spots/0/tip: The shops in the departures area are small, so buy souvenirs ahead of time at Ichibangai, the underground mall at Okayama Station
spots/0/kid_tip: You can watch the planes from the observation deck on the 2nd floor
spots/1/desc: The starting point for your trip, where the Shinkansen, local trains, streetcars and airport buses all meet. Sanste Okayama inside the station and the underground Ichibangai are packed with restaurants and souvenir shops, which makes them good for shopping before you leave.
spots/1/tip: The Momotaro statue in front of the east exit is a landmark near the streetcar and bus stops
spots/1/kid_tip: Take a souvenir photo in front of the Momotaro statue at the east exit
spots/2/desc: A spacious lawn garden counted among Japan's three great gardens, along with Kenrokuen in Kanazawa and Kairakuen in Mito. The classic photo spot is the view of Okayama Castle's keep beyond the pond.
spots/2/access: Take the streetcar from Okayama Station to Joshita and walk 10 minutes, or take a bus to Korakuen-mae
spots/2/tip: A combined ticket with Okayama Castle is a little cheaper (to be confirmed). During the summer night opening, the "Fantasy Garden" (Genso Teien), you can also come back in the evening
spots/2/kid_tip: The wide lawns are great for running around, and kibi dango (millet dumplings) are sold next to the tea house
spots/3/desc: Its black outer walls earned it the nickname "Crow Castle." After renovations in 2022, the inside of the keep became an interactive exhibit. It connects to Korakuen via the Tsukimi Bridge, so it is easy to see both in one go.
spots/3/access: Get off the streetcar at Joshita and walk 10 minutes
spots/3/tip: Inside the keep you can try a palanquin ride and traditional costumes, and the view from the top is great
spots/3/kid_tip: The exhibits inside are set at a child's eye level, and there is a Bizen ware making experience (reservation required)
spots/4/desc: A small museum housing armor, swords and Noh costumes of the Ikeda family, the lords of Okayama. It is right next to Okayama Castle, so 30 minutes is enough when combined with a castle visit.
spots/4/closed: Mondays (next day if a national holiday), year-end and New Year holidays (to be confirmed)
spots/4/tip: It closes on some days while exhibits are being changed, so check before you go
spots/5/desc: A museum with works by local artists such as Okayama native Urakami Gyokudo and Sesshu, and it often hosts special exhibitions. It is a 10-minute walk from Korakuen and Okayama Castle, so it fits well into a rainy-day itinerary.
spots/5/access: Get off the streetcar at Joshita and walk 3 minutes
spots/5/closed: Mondays (next day if a national holiday), year-end and New Year holidays
spots/5/tip: Special exhibitions cost extra. The permanent collection alone is around ¥350 (to be confirmed)
spots/6/desc: A covered shopping arcade running north to south on the west side of Okayama Castle. Old Western-style restaurants, ramen shops and souvenir stores are mixed together, so it is easy to walk even in the rain.
spots/6/access: Right at the Kencho-dori streetcar stop
spots/6/tip: Buy fruit and Japanese sweets at the food hall in the basement of the Tenmaya department store at the south end
spots/7/desc: A large shopping mall a 5-minute walk from Okayama Station, with drugstores, Uniqlo and a food court all in one building. It is handy on rainy days, for shopping before you leave, and for meals with children.
spots/7/access: 5-minute walk from the east exit of Okayama Station
spots/7/tip: The food court on the 5th floor and the rooftop garden are good places to rest with kids
spots/7/kid_tip: There is an indoor play area and diaper changing tables on every floor
spots/8/desc: The main hall, a National Treasure, enshrines Kibitsuhiko-no-Mikoto, the model for the Momotaro legend, and the nearly 400 m long corridor that follows the foot of the hill is stunning. The shrine is also famous for the Narukama Shinji, a fortune-telling ritual based on the sound of a boiling cauldron.
spots/8/access: 10-minute walk from Kibitsu Station on the JR Kibi Line
spots/8/tip: The corridor is most photogenic when the morning light slants in. The hydrangea garden blooms in May and June
spots/8/kid_tip: They sell omamori (charms) with a Momotaro picture
spots/9/desc: The leading shrine of Bizen Province, enshrining the same deity as Kibitsu Shrine. It is known as the "Asahi Shrine" because on the summer solstice the morning sun rises straight in front of the approach. The spacious grounds, with a large stone lantern and a pond, are good for a stroll.
spots/9/access: 3-minute walk from Bizen-Ichinomiya Station on the JR Kibi Line
spots/9/tip: Rent a bicycle in front of Bizen-Ichinomiya Station and ride the flat paddy-field road to Kibitsu Shrine in 25 minutes
spots/9/kid_tip: Feed the carp in the pond on the grounds
spots/10/desc: A large temple counted among Japan's three great Inari shrines, notable for its 27 m tall torii gate and a distinctive Indian-style main hall. Small shops along the approach sell inari sushi and souvenirs.
spots/10/access: 5 minutes by taxi or 30 minutes on foot from Bitchu-Takamatsu Station on the JR line, or 10 minutes by taxi from Kibitsu Shrine
spots/10/hours: Grounds always open (main hall 5:30–17:00, to be confirmed)
spots/10/tip: It gets very crowded over the New Year holidays, so avoid that time
spots/11/desc: The gateway to Kurashiki, just 17 minutes from Okayama by JR. It is a 12-minute walk from the south exit to the Bikan Historical Quarter, and Mitsui Outlet Park is right in front of the north exit.
spots/11/access: 17 minutes (¥330) on the JR Sanyo Main Line from Okayama Station
spots/11/tip: Pick up a Korean-language map at the tourist information center by the south exit
spots/12/desc: A district where Edo-period rice storehouses and white-walled, black-tiled merchant houses still line the canal. With willows draping over the water, little boats, and cafes and craft studios in the lanes, half a day passes quickly.
spots/12/access: 12-minute walk from the south exit of Kurashiki Station
spots/12/tip: It is quiet and photogenic before 10 a.m. or around dusk. After sunset the area is lit up until 21:00 (22:00 in some seasons)
spots/12/kid_tip: The canal boat and the Momotaro Karakuri Museum are popular with kids
spots/13/desc: Japan's first museum of Western modern art, opened in 1930, with works such as El Greco's "The Annunciation" and Monet's "Water Lilies." The Greek temple-style main gallery, the craft and Asian galleries, and the annex are scattered through the Bikan Quarter.
spots/13/access: 15-minute walk from Kurashiki Station, at the canal entrance of the Bikan Quarter
spots/13/closed: Mondays (open if a national holiday), year-end and New Year holidays
spots/13/tip: The main gallery alone takes an hour. The annex may have been reorganized since 2025, so follow the on-site signs for the route (to be confirmed)
spots/13/kid_tip: Free for elementary school children and younger (to be confirmed)
spots/14/desc: A red-brick complex where a Meiji-era spinning mill, ivy and all, was turned into a hotel, plaza and craft studios. The plaza benches and the Bizen ware workshop make it a nice place to take a break.
spots/14/access: 5-minute walk from the Bikan Quarter canal
spots/14/tip: A beer garden opens in the plaza on summer evenings
spots/14/kid_tip: Hand-wheel pottery with Bizen ware clay (30 minutes, reservation recommended)
spots/15/desc: A folk craft museum made by joining four rice storehouses, displaying everyday craft items such as pottery, textiles and baskets. The storehouse building is itself worth seeing, which makes it a good stop on a rainy day.
spots/15/access: 3-minute walk from the Ohara Museum of Art
spots/15/closed: Mondays (next day if a national holiday)
spots/15/tip: The baskets and pottery at the shop by the entrance make good gifts
spots/16/desc: A small boat poled by a boatman in a straw hat makes a 20-minute round trip along the Bikan Quarter canal. The white walls and willows look different from the water as you look up at them.
spots/16/access: Buy tickets at the Kurashiki-kan tourist information center beside the canal
spots/16/closed: 2nd Monday of the month from March to November, weekdays from December to February (to be confirmed)
spots/16/tip: On weekends and holidays the same-day tickets sell out in the morning, so buy them as soon as you arrive
spots/16/kid_tip: Recommended for ages 5 and up, life jackets provided
spots/17/desc: A small interactive museum that retells the Momotaro legend through optical illusions and trick devices, with an ogre cave adventure as the highlight. It takes 30 minutes to go through and kids love it.
spots/17/access: 2-minute walk from the Bikan Quarter canal
spots/17/tip: There are dark sections, so hold the hand of any child who gets scared easily
spots/17/kid_tip: Children ¥400. In the last room you can take a photo dressed up as Momotaro
spots/18/desc: A narrow lane in the Bikan Quarter lined with shops selling Kojima denim accessories. It is known for photo-friendly treats such as denim soft-serve ice cream and denim-colored manju.
spots/18/access: 3-minute walk from the Ohara Museum of Art
spots/18/tip: For real jeans, go to Kojima Jeans Street. For small goods and gifts, come here
spots/19/desc: An outlet mall right in front of the north exit of Kurashiki Station, with plenty of sportswear and children's clothing stores. It connects to the neighboring Ario Kurashiki, so it is a good way to spend half a day when it rains.
spots/19/access: 3-minute walk from the north exit of Kurashiki Station
spots/19/tip: There is a tax-free counter. Bring your passport
spots/19/kid_tip: Ario has a food court and a lawn plaza
spots/20/desc: About 40 denim brand shops are gathered along the old shopping street of Kojima, the birthplace of Japanese-made jeans. Jeans-shaped decorations hanging over the street are its symbol, and each shop can do alterations and custom orders.
spots/20/access: 15 minutes on foot or 5 minutes by bus from Kojima Station on the JR line
spots/20/closed: Varies by shop (many are closed on Wednesdays, to be confirmed)
spots/20/tip: Jeans start from around ¥20,000. Many places can do alterations the same day
spots/21/desc: A hilltop viewpoint 133 m above sea level with a sweeping view of the Great Seto Bridge and the islands, regarded as the best sunset spot on the Seto Inland Sea. It is a 15-minute walk on a trail from the parking lot to the top.
spots/21/access: 20 minutes by Shimoden bus from Kojima Station on the JR line (get off at Washuzan Dai-ni Observation Deck)
spots/21/tip: Arrive 30 minutes before sunset. Return buses are infrequent, so take a photo of the timetable ahead of time
spots/22/desc: A 1 km long white-sand beach, a rare sight on the Seto Inland Sea, used for swimming in summer and as a walking route in other seasons. The Shibukawa Marine Aquarium is right next to it.
spots/22/access: 25 minutes by bus from Kojima Station on the JR line, or by rental car
spots/22/tip: Outside the July to August swimming season it is quiet
spots/22/kid_tip: The shallow sandy beach is safe for playing in the water, and there is a small aquarium
spots/23/desc: An olive farm on the hills of Ushimado, nicknamed the "Aegean Sea of Japan," where the observation deck looks down on the Seto Inland Sea dotted with islands. It has a shop for olive oil and cosmetics and a cafe with a view.
spots/23/access: 20 minutes by bus from Oku Station on the JR line to Ushimado, then a 30-minute walk or 5 minutes by taxi
spots/23/tip: The classic photo spot is in front of the "Bell of Happiness" on the hill. The afternoon light is from behind the view, so visit between morning and noon
spots/24/desc: A harbor town where the Joseon Korean envoys once stayed, with a seaside promenade, a yacht harbor and old streets still in place. Ferries to nearby Maejima run every 10 minutes.
spots/24/access: 20 minutes by Tobi bus from Oku Station on the JR line
spots/24/tip: See the full harbor view from the hill behind Honrenji Temple. The Joseon Envoy Museum (Kaiyu Bunkakan) is also worth a stop
spots/25/desc: Dozens of kilns and galleries for Bizen ware, which is fired in a wood-burning kiln without glaze, line the streets in front of the station. At the Bizen Ware Traditional Industry Hall you can compare and buy works by different artists in one place.
spots/25/access: Right in front of Imbe Station on the JR Ako Line (40 minutes from Okayama)
spots/25/closed: Traditional Industry Hall closed Tuesdays (to be confirmed)
spots/25/tip: Beer mugs and tea cups start at around ¥5,000. The Bizen Ware Festival is held on the third weekend of October
spots/26/desc: It displays famous swords from Osafune, a former center of Japanese sword making, and in the neighboring workshop you can watch the swordsmiths at work. For anyone interested in Japanese swords, it is the most special place in Okayama.
spots/26/access: 7 minutes by taxi from Osafune Station on the JR line (rental car recommended)
spots/26/closed: Mondays (next day if a national holiday), during exhibit changes
spots/26/tip: Workshop demonstrations are open to the public on the second Sunday of each month (to be confirmed)
spots/27/desc: A fruit farm north of Okayama city that offers white peach picking in July and August and Kyoho and Muscat grape picking from August to October. At the direct-sales shop you can buy seasonal fruit and fruit desserts.
spots/27/access: 30 minutes by rental car or taxi from Okayama Station (public transport is inconvenient, to be confirmed)
spots/27/closed: Picking is closed outside the harvest season (to be confirmed)
spots/27/tip: Reservations are required for picking. Prices vary by fruit and season (to be confirmed)
spots/27/kid_tip: There is little shade, so bring hats and water
spots/28/desc: The only mountain castle in Japan with an original keep still standing, 430 m above sea level, and on autumn mornings it can be seen floating above a sea of clouds. You have to walk 20 minutes up a mountain path from the parking lot to the keep.
spots/28/access: Shuttle bus or taxi from Bitchu-Takahashi Station on the JR line, or a rental car, then a 20-minute walk
spots/28/tip: The sea of clouds appears at dawn from late September to early April, and the viewpoint is in a separate location. Comfortable shoes are a must
spots/29/desc: The ruins of a 7th-century ancient mountain fortress, where the restored west gate and walls offer a full view of the Kibi Plain. It is said to be the castle where the ogres lived in the Momotaro legend.
spots/29/access: By rental car (10-minute walk from the visitor center parking lot). Public transport is inconvenient
spots/29/closed: Visitor center closed Mondays (to be confirmed)
spots/29/tip: The mountain road is narrow, so choose a small rental car
restaurants/0/signature: Demi-katsu don (pork cutlet rice bowl with demi-glace sauce)
restaurants/0/desc: A long-established restaurant founded in 1931 and considered the originator of Okayama's signature demi-katsu don. The pork cutlet on a bed of cabbage and the sweet demi-glace sauce suit children's tastes too.
restaurants/0/tips/0: Expect a line at the lunch peak
restaurants/0/tips/1: The amount of sauce can be adjusted
restaurants/1/signature: Ebimeshi (shrimp fried rice with sauce) set
restaurants/1/desc: A leading shop for ebimeshi, Okayama-style shrimp fried rice stir-fried in a dark sauce. The set paired with an omelet rice and a salad is popular, and many family customers come.
restaurants/1/tips/0: 10 minutes by taxi from the station. There is also a Mannari branch
restaurants/2/desc: A restaurant inside the station where you can eat Okayama's local barazushi and sushi made with Seto Inland Sea fish. It fits your route well for a last meal before the airport or a first meal right after you arrive.
restaurants/2/tips/1: A course menu is also offered in the evening
restaurants/3/desc: A long-established shop on the Hokancho shopping street west of the station, with barazushi topped with Seto Inland Sea fish such as sawara (Spanish mackerel) and mamakari as its signature dish. It is also a good choice for a local-cuisine course dinner.
restaurants/3/tips/1: No Korean menu, but there is a menu with photos
restaurants/4/desc: A long-established shop founded in 1950 and a leading name in Okayama ramen, known for its clear, light broth of chicken bones and soy sauce. It stays open late, so it works for dinner or a late-night bowl.
restaurants/4/tips/0: Not spicy, so kids can eat it too
restaurants/5/signature: Chuka soba and demi-katsu don set
restaurants/5/desc: A long-established ramen and Western-style restaurant near Omotecho where you can have ramen and demi-katsu don in one sitting, making it a good introduction to Okayama specialties. Many local office workers eat here.
restaurants/5/tips/0: Dinner service is short, so go early
restaurants/5/tips/1: Portions are large, so share the set
restaurants/6/signature: Chicken karaage and Seto Inland Sea sashimi
restaurants/6/desc: A large izakaya in front of Okayama Station with a good range of chicken dishes, sashimi and local sake. With plenty of seats, it is easy for families to walk in without a reservation.
restaurants/7/desc: A leading roastery cafe in the Tonyacho district, a warehouse street that has been renovated. Select shops and bakeries nearby make it easy to pair with an afternoon stroll.
restaurants/7/tips/0: 15 minutes by bus from Okayama Station
restaurants/8/desc: The main store of Otemanju, Okayama's best-known Japanese sweet, in business since 1837. You can buy freshly steamed manju one at a time, so it makes a good snack during a stroll around Okayama Castle.
restaurants/8/tips/0: You can also buy them at the station and department stores, but at the main store they are freshly steamed
restaurants/9/signature: Udon, ramen, hamburgers and more, your choice
restaurants/9/desc: A food court with high chairs and roomy seating, where each family member can pick what they want to eat. It is convenient on rainy days or for a quick meal before heading to the airport.
restaurants/9/tips/0: 5th floor. Baby food can be warmed up
restaurants/10/signature: Bukkake udon (cold noodles with a rich tsuyu broth)
restaurants/10/desc: The original shop for Kurashiki's signature bukkake udon, where chewy noodles are served with a lightly sweet tsuyu poured over them. It is inexpensive and quick, making it a good lunch between sights in the Bikan Quarter.
restaurants/10/tips/0: Hot versions can also be ordered
restaurants/10/tips/1: There is also a main branch in front of the station
restaurants/11/desc: A restaurant in an old storehouse building serving mamakari, Okayama's local fish dish, and barazushi. It has both floor seating and tables, and the set-meal format makes ordering easy.
restaurants/11/tips/1: Barazushi is a safe choice for children
restaurants/12/desc: A 1950s Western-style restaurant next to the Ohara Museum of Art, focused on kid-friendly dishes such as beef stew, hayashi rice and omelet rice. Some seats look out over the canal.
restaurants/12/tips/0: The lunch set is a good value
restaurants/13/desc: A cafe that preserves an Edo-period merchant house, with its earthen-floor entryway and inner courtyard intact. It is famous for its seasonal fruit parfait, and the lunch curry is good too.
restaurants/13/tips/0: On weekends the wait is 30 minutes or more
restaurants/13/tips/1: Visiting right after opening in the morning is recommended
restaurants/14/signature: Seto Inland Sea fruit parfait (white peach and Muscat)
restaurants/14/desc: A fruit specialty cafe famous for parfaits topped with whole Okayama fruit. White peaches go on top in summer and Muscat and Kyoho grapes in autumn, and there are several branches in the Bikan Quarter.
restaurants/14/tips/1: If the line is long, try the Chuo branch or the Bikan Quarter branch
restaurants/15/desc: An ivy-covered coffee house that opened in 1959, right next to the Ohara Museum of Art. The high ceiling and wooden chairs are unchanged, making it a nice place to rest before or after the museum.
restaurants/16/desc: A canal-side coffee house that roasts its own beans and has stuck with flannel drip since 1971. It is a small shop with few seats, but coffee lovers should not miss it.
restaurants/16/tips/1: Preschool-age children may find it hard to sit quietly
restaurants/17/signature: Seasonal Seto Inland Sea kaiseki course
restaurants/17/desc: Lunch and dinner kaiseki served by reservation at a renowned ryokan in the Bikan Quarter, open to guests who are not staying there. It is made with Seto Inland Sea fish and Okayama vegetables, and suits an evening on a special occasion.
restaurants/17/hours: Lunch 11:30–14:00, dinner from 18:00 (by reservation, to be confirmed)
restaurants/17/tips/1: The lunch course is relatively cheaper
restaurants/18/desc: A shrimp specialty restaurant on the seaside near Ushimado, famous for its set meal of large fried shrimp. It is a good lunch stop to pair with the Olive Garden and Ushimado Harbor.
restaurants/18/tips/0: Long waits on weekends, so arriving before opening is recommended
restaurants/19/desc: A leading shop for kakioko, the specialty of the fishing port of Hinase, grilling okonomiyaki piled high with winter-season oysters on the griddle. Outside oyster season it operates with frozen oysters.
restaurants/19/tips/0: Weekends from November to March mean a 1-hour wait
restaurants/19/tips/1: Realistic only with the rental car plan
hotels/0/desc: A JR-group hotel directly connected to Okayama Station, with the airport bus, JR and streetcar all at its door. The rooms are spacious and the breakfast is good, so it is a safe first choice for any itinerary.
hotels/0/pts/0: Connected to the station, minimal luggage hauling
hotels/0/pts/1: Spacious rooms and a breakfast buffet
hotels/0/pts/2: A base for day trips to Kurashiki and Kojima
hotels/1/name: Natural Hot Spring Kibi no Yu Dormy Inn Okayama
hotels/1/desc: A business hotel, 7 minutes on foot from the station, popular for its natural hot spring public bath on the top floor and free late-night ramen (yonaki soba). It offers great value for the price.
hotels/1/pts/0: Natural hot spring public bath and sauna
hotels/1/pts/1: Free late-night ramen and a local-style breakfast
hotels/1/pts/2: Located between the station and the shopping streets
hotels/2/desc: A red-brick hotel converted from an old spinning mill, and its biggest charm is that you stay inside the Bikan Quarter. You can enjoy an evening stroll and the quiet canal in the early morning.
hotels/2/pts/1: The atmosphere of the ivy-covered courtyard
hotels/2/pts/2: Right next to the Bizen ware workshop
hotels/3/desc: An upscale ryokan with just 8 rooms right beside the Bikan Quarter canal, with a Seto Inland Sea kaiseki dinner included. It suits a special anniversary trip.
hotels/3/pts/2: Few rooms, so it is quiet
hotels/4/desc: A city hotel at the entrance of the Bikan Quarter with triple and family rooms, within walking distance of the station. The museums and canal are 5 minutes on foot, so it is easy to go back and forth briefly with children.
hotels/4/pts/2: Breakfast buffet and a spacious lobby
hotels/5/desc: A hot spring hotel by the sea at the foot of Washuzan, where the open-air bath and the rooms overlook the Great Seto Bridge and the islands. It has a children's play area, so it is popular with families too.
hotels/5/pts/0: Hot spring with a view of the Great Seto Bridge
hotels/6/desc: A resort hotel in a white Greek-style building next to the Ushimado yacht harbor, with every room facing the sea. It is a good one-night stay on the Ushimado and Bizen side with the rental car plan.
hotels/6/pts/2: 5 minutes by car from the Olive Garden
plans/0/theme: Gardens and castle, a white-walled canal town, and the Momotaro shrine
plans/0/summary: See Okayama Castle and Korakuen on the first day, spend all of day two in the Kurashiki Bikan Quarter, and visit Kibitsu Shrine on the last day before heading to the airport. You stay at one hotel in front of Okayama Station, so there is no luggage to move.
plans/0/days/0/kicker: From castle to garden across one bridge
plans/0/days/0/note: Leave your bags at the hotel first and head out light. Korakuen is at its prettiest about an hour before sunset.
plans/0/days/0/items/0/note: Head to the limousine bus stop in front of the arrivals lobby
plans/0/days/0/items/2/note: Drop your bags at the hotel and go out the east exit
plans/0/days/0/items/3/note: Start with Okayama's specialty, demi-katsu don, or barazushi
plans/0/days/0/items/4/text: Higashiyama Line 5 min · ¥120, get off at Joshita and walk 10 min
plans/0/days/0/items/7/note: Take photos with the keep across the pond
plans/0/days/0/items/8/text: 10 min from the Korakuen-mae stop to Okayama Station · about ¥200
plans/0/days/0/items/9/note: Check in, take a short rest
plans/0/days/0/items/10/note: A local barazushi course, or an izakaya in front of the station
plans/0/days/0/items/11/text: Buy snacks and drinks at the underground Ichibangai or AEON Mall
plans/0/days/1/title: All day in the white-walled canal town
plans/0/days/1/note: Go early in the morning to enjoy the quiet. In the afternoon, rest at cafes, then see the canal lights at dusk before heading back.
plans/0/days/1/notice/t: The Ohara Museum of Art and the Folk Craft Museum are closed on Mondays (open if a national holiday). If it is a Monday, swap this with day 1.
plans/0/days/1/items/1/note: Pick up a map at the tourist information center by the south exit
plans/0/days/1/items/3/note: A loop along the canal, take photos when it is less crowded
plans/0/days/1/items/4/note: An hour and a half, focusing on the main gallery
plans/0/days/1/items/5/note: Bukkake udon is fast, and Kiyutei has plenty of kids' dishes
plans/0/days/1/items/6/note: Stroll the brick courtyard, and try a Bizen ware workshop if you like
plans/0/days/1/items/7/note: 20-minute boat ride, buy tickets in the morning in advance
plans/0/days/1/items/8/note: Denim goods and denim ice cream
plans/0/days/1/items/9/note: Momoko for a seasonal fruit parfait, Miyake for the atmosphere
plans/0/days/1/items/10/note: Shop at the outlets and Ario on the way back to the station
